sentences.text: Yes, the supplied evidence supports an association between rheumatoid arthritis and periodontal disease.

In 1,412 individuals attending the University of Queensland's School of Dentistry, self-reported rheumatoid arthritis prevalence was 3.95% among patients referred for advanced periodontal care versus 0.66% in those not referred and 1% in the general population.
Among referred patients with rheumatoid arthritis, 62.5% had advanced forms of periodontal disease.
The passage shows an association, but because it relies on self-report and dental records, it does not establish causality.
The evidence is insufficient to determine whether delayed gastric emptying after pancreaticoduodenectomy is related to pylorus preservation.

One study of 51 patients undergoing pylorus-preserving pancreaticoduodenectomy reported an overall DGE incidence of 12%, with DGE occurring in 3% of patients without other postoperative complications versus 30% of those with other complications (P=0.002).

That passage also states DGE is the most frequent postoperative complication after pylorus-preserving pancreaticoduodenectomy, but it does not compare pylorus preservation with non-preserving resection.
Other supplied passages mention pylorus-preserving resection or technique but provide no DGE outcomes or comparison.

Yes—senior final-year medical students can contribute to day-surgery quality assurance, as their case follow-up identified problems and generated recommendations and new guidelines/protocols. In an audit of 59 final-year medical students who followed allocated patients through all phases of day surgery, students documented 621 cases, a sampling of 14.1% of day surgery cases. Their contributions included highlighting inappropriate patient and procedure selection, inadequate pain management, discharge, communication, and resource issues, and recommending multilingual videotapes/information sheets, avoidance of bilateral procedures, and improved links with local medical officers. The passages describe a single educational/audit programme without a comparison group, so they support feasibility and contribution but do not quantify impact on QA outcomes.
Yes—inhaled corticosteroids appear to reduce perception of dyspnea during bronchoconstriction in asthma, based on lower VAS dyspnea scores in ICS-treated patients.

In 100 asthma patients during a 5–20% methacholine-induced fall in FEV1, VAS score was lowest in obstructed ICS-treated patients (group II), slightly higher in obstructed ICS-naive patients (group I), higher still in nonobstructed ICS-treated patients (group IV), and highest in nonobstructed ICS-naive patients (group III).

Post hoc analysis showed that in ICS-treated patients eosinophil counts and bronchial hyperresponsiveness were negatively associated with perception of dyspnea, whereas in ICS-naive patients eosinophil counts were positively associated with it.
The study is observational and does not report a randomized ICS-versus-placebo comparison of dyspnea perception.
Yes, the supplied evidence indicates endothelin-1 is an aggravating factor in acute pancreatitis, based on a rat model in which ETA receptor blockade reduced hemorrhagic pancreatitis severity.

In rats given cerulein plus 5-hour restraint water-immersion stress, all untreated animals developed acute hemorrhagic pancreatitis with a pancreatic hemorrhage score of 2.4 ± 0.2, whereas BQ123-pretreated rats had a reduced score of 1.0 ± 0.0, significantly lower pancreas wet weight and serum amylase, and improved local pancreatic blood flow.
The same report also cites prior evidence that endothelin-1 administration transformed cerulein-induced edematous pancreatitis into hemorrhagic pancreatitis in rats.
The evidence is limited to this animal model and does not establish human relevance or whether endothelin-1 initiates pancreatitis.
The evidence is mixed: year of radical prostatectomy was a predictor of outcome in preoperative analysis but not in postoperative analysis.

In 6,556 patients from 7 centers who underwent radical prostatectomy between 1985 and 2000 (median follow-up 23 months), RP year was significant on preoperative Cox multivariate analysis (p = 0.006) but not on postoperative analysis (p = 0.130).
Outcome improved with surgery through the mid-1990s and then appeared to level off.
Other supplied passages examined other prognostic factors, such as PSA, tumor length, high-grade cancer, palpable cancer extent, and ethnicity/risk group, but did not assess RP year.
The evidence is mixed and does not settle whether extended aortic replacement in acute type A dissection is justifiable.

In 411 patients with type A dissection undergoing arch replacement, a stented elephant trunk compared with conventional repair had lower in-hospital mortality in acute dissection (4.73% vs 6.06%) and false-lumen obliteration around the stent in 94.2% of acute cases, but higher spinal cord injury (2.41% vs 0.83%) and stroke (2.41% vs 0.83%).
That study excluded subtotal or total aortic replacement, so it does not directly answer whether more extensive aortic replacement is justified.
Two acute type A dissection patients developed severe haemolytic anaemia after elephant-trunk aortic surgery, including one after total arch replacement, requiring further surgery.
Another source notes high morbidity/mortality and complications in surgically treated aortic dissection and asks whether a more conservative approach is sometimes justified.

The evidence is mixed/insufficient to determine whether normal knee kinematics are restored with unicompartmental knee replacement: one clinical study found mean interlimb symmetry but frequent individual asymmetry, while a cadaver study testing unchanged kinematics provided no results in the supplied passages.

In 17 medial and 9 lateral UKA patients with nondiseased contralateral limbs, stair-ascent kinematics showed no clinically meaningful mean interlimb differences (threshold 5°), but about half in each group were asymmetric favoring either the operated or nonoperated limb.

A separate cadaver study of six knees compared kinematics before implantation, after a bicruciate-retaining unicompartmental prosthesis, and after a posterior cruciate-retaining tricompartmental prosthesis under simulated stair climbing, but the supplied passages do not report whether kinematics were unchanged.

The evidence is insufficient to determine whether minilaparoscopic inguinal hernia repair is feasible, because the only relevant passage describes a retrospective initial experience of minilaparoscopic transabdominal preperitoneal (miniTAPP) repair of groin hernia defects at two institutions but reports no feasibility outcomes.
That study did not provide patient numbers, comparison groups, or success rates.

Other supplied passages address standard laparoscopic repair for incarcerated abdominal hernias (2688 laparoscopic vs 15,562 open) , day-case elective inguinal hernia repair in elderly patients , and laparoscopic inguinal hernia repair in infants and children , but none evaluate minilaparoscopic inguinal hernia repair.
Therefore, the available passages do not settle the question.
The evidence is mixed on whether half-dose contrast-enhanced 3D MR angiography is sufficient for the abdominal aorta and pelvis.

In 72 patients randomized to different gadolinium concentrations, total amounts (single or half-dose), and injection rates (1 or 0.5 mL/sec), overall image quality differences across the four groups were not statistically significant.
However, SNR and CNR of the abdominal aorta and common iliac artery were significantly lower in the 0.5 mL/sec groups than in the 1 mL/sec groups.
The study evaluated the abdominal aorta and its major branches, including common and external iliac arteries, but did not isolate the half-dose effect on pelvic image quality.

Yes, some do: in 59 women with synchronous endometrial and ovarian cancers who had tumor blocks analyzed, 2 met Amsterdam criteria for HNPCC and 5 additional medium-risk women had molecular findings consistent with a germline MSH2 or MLH1 mutation, while none of the low-risk women had such findings.
Thus, Lynch syndrome is present in a subset of these women, particularly those with high- or medium-risk family histories, rather than in all of them.
Yes—rural residence was associated with worse neonatal outcome in very premature birth, based on higher adjusted mortality among rural infants.

In New South Wales/Australian Capital Territory, 1879 rural and 6775 urban infants <32 weeks gestational age admitted to all 10 neonatal intensive care units in 1992–2002 had adjusted mortality odds ratio 1.26 (95% CI 1.07–1.48, p=0.005) for rural residence.
Urban infants were more often born in a tertiary obstetric hospital (93% vs 83%), and regional data also showed a higher stillbirth rate among rural infants (OR 1.20, 95% CI 1.09–1.32, p<0.001).

The evidence is mixed: in one pretest-posttest controlled study, counter sampling plus pharmacist education was associated with a significant decrease in COX-2 NSAID prescribing but not with decreases in nonsedating antihistamine or PPI prescribing.
The study compared 8 medical providers at an active-intervention clinic with 7 providers at a control clinic in two rural southeastern Idaho immediate-care settings.
At the intervention site, COX-2 NSAIDs fell from 38.9% to 23.7% of total NSAID prescriptions (P<0.05), while the control site had a nonstatistically significant decrease from 67.5% to 62% (P>0.05).

However, the intervention group significantly increased focus-nonsedating antihistamines (86.7% to 93.1%) and PPIs (68.9% to 86.2%) as percentages of total yearly prescriptions (P<0.05 for each), and the control group also increased these categories significantly.
Because the groups differed significantly at baseline in all three medication categories, the reported comparisons emphasize within-group changes rather than between-group differences.
Evidence is mixed: in pT3 renal cell carcinoma, tumour VEGF expression was independently associated with survival but was not significantly associated with venous invasion.
In 78 patients with pT3a/pT3b tumours without vena cava invasion or pT3b tumours with vena cava invasion, VEGF expression did not differ significantly between the groups; only tumour size did.

On univariate analysis VEGF expression was significantly associated with survival (p<0.01), and on multivariate analysis it remained an independent predictor (OR 6.07) along with lymph node involvement and distant metastases.

No clear association is supported: in a large study, women with recurrent spontaneous abortion had an extreme X-inactivation skewing rate of 8.6%, which was not statistically different from infertility, spontaneous-abortion, or multiparous groups.
The recurrent-loss group did differ from primiparous women (8.6% vs 1.0%, P<.01), but this was the only significant comparison.

Within the recurrent-loss group, extreme skewing was also not significantly related to prior live birth (9.9% with at least one live birth vs 5.6% with no live births and at least three losses, P>.05).
Other supplied passages do not address skewed X-inactivation.
No — routine in-depth investigation of cholestasis in small bowel atresia does not appear always necessary.

In a retrospective review of 53 patients with small bowel atresia, 24 (45%) developed postoperative cholestasis; 10 (36%) proceeded with in-depth evaluations and 8 (28%) underwent liver biopsy, but no patient had biliary atresia.
Cholestasis resolved spontaneously in all survivors, and no deaths were related to isolated cholestasis or cirrhosis.
These findings suggest that cholestasis in this population can be managed without always pursuing invasive investigation, though the evidence comes from a retrospective single-series review.
No, in the only supplied study directly addressing this, SGA was not associated with increased ROP risk.
Among 345 preterm infants (BW ≤1,500 g, GA ≤32 weeks), any-stage ROP occurred in 24.7% of SGA vs 33.2% of AGA (p=0.111), and severe ROP in 6.2% vs 7.5% (p=0.779).
Adjusted analysis identified weight gain from birth to sixth week and need for blood transfusions, not SGA, as significant ROP risk factors.

No — manual resuscitators do not reliably deliver accurate tidal volumes, because volume delivery varies significantly with squeezing technique and most measured breaths fall outside recommended ranges.

In 114 BLS-trained individuals using a manual resuscitator connected to a microspirometer, mean tidal volumes were 592.84 mL (SD 117.39) one-handed, 644.24 mL (SD 144.7) two-handed, and 458.31 mL (SD 120.91) two-handed half-compression (p<0.01), and two-handed delivery was greater than one-handed (r=0.398, p<0.01).
Hand size, hand volume, and grip power did not correlate with delivered volume, while education/practice showed only weak correlations (r=0.213, 0.281, 0.131; p<0.01).

In 50 urban EMS providers, only 17.5% of pediatric-bag-valve-mask breaths and 5.1% of adult-bag-valve-mask breaths were within the recommended tidal volume range (p<0.001), with median volumes of 570.5, 664.0, and 663.0 mL for pediatric BVM versus 796.0, 994.5, and 981.5 mL for adult BVM (p<0.001).
Thus, the supplied evidence shows poor accuracy and high variability rather than reliable accurate tidal-volume delivery by manual resuscitator.
The evidence is insufficient to conclude that telmisartan prevents hepatic fibrosis in rats with alloxan-induced diabetes.

In 15 adult male rats, alloxan-induced diabetic rats treated with telmisartan 10 mg/kg/day for 30 days showed no TGF-beta immunoreactivity in liver sections, whereas the diabetic control group was strongly immunoreactive to TGF-beta.
The study also reported a significant difference in hepatocyte numerical density between the diabetic control and telmisartan-treated diabetic groups.
However, the passages do not report direct histological fibrosis scoring or collagen quantification, so they show reduced TGF-beta staining but do not establish prevention of hepatic fibrosis.
The evidence is insufficient to conclude that preventing osteoporosis is the key to eliminating aromatase inhibitor-related musculoskeletal symptoms.

In a retrospective review of 316 patients with hormone receptor-positive nonmetastatic breast cancer treated with an aromatase inhibitor for ≥3 months and with DEXA data, musculoskeletal symptoms were significantly associated with DEXA-BMD (P<.001), and the group receiving calcium/bisphosphonate had more patients without musculoskeletal symptoms and fewer fractures.

However, that study was observational and did not test whether preventing osteoporosis eliminates symptoms; it also found fewer symptoms and fractures in patients who received tamoxifen before aromatase inhibitors and more symptoms and fractures with steroidal versus nonsteroidal aromatase inhibitors.

The other supplied passages address bone density or musculoskeletal disorders in rheumatoid arthritis, inflammatory bowel disease, primary biliary cirrhosis/hepatitis C cirrhosis, and general populations, not aromatase inhibitor-related symptoms.

No, higher BMI was not associated with worse asthma control in the urban population studied, as regression analysis showed no association between obesity or increasing BMI and asthma control on any of four validated questionnaires.
The study included 292 patients with asthma (mean age 47 years; 82% women, 67% African American) recruited from primary care, with 63% obese and only 15% normal weight.
Mean asthma control scores were suboptimal: ACCI 8.3/19, ACT 15.4/25, ACQ 2.1/6, and ATAQ 1.3/4.
The lack of association persisted after adjusting for FEV1, smoking status, race, sex, selected comorbid illnesses, and long-term controller use.
Yes, elective re-siting of intravenous cannulae every 48 hours decreased peripheral thrombophlebitis in a small randomized trial.

In 42 patients admitted for major abdominal surgery receiving intravenous fluids/drugs, 21 control patients had cannulae removed only for pain, dislodgement, or signs of thrombophlebitis, while 21 study patients had cannulae changed and re-sited every 48 hours.
The incidence of peripheral venous thrombophlebitis was 100% (21/21) in the control group versus 9.5% (2/21) in the study group, p<0.0001, and severity was also lower in the study group.
Day-wise correlation showed 82.6% of thrombophlebitis episodes occurred on day 3.

Yes, meta-analytic evidence indicates progressive structural brain changes in schizophrenia. In 27 longitudinal region-of-interest MRI studies including 928 patients and 867 healthy controls followed for 1 to 10 years, patients showed significantly greater decreases over time in whole brain, whole-brain gray matter, frontal gray and white matter, parietal white matter, and temporal white matter volume, plus larger increases in lateral ventricular volume. The annualized percentage differences versus controls were -.07% for whole brain volume, -.59% for whole-brain gray matter, -.32% for frontal white matter, -.32% for parietal white matter, -.39% for temporal white matter, and +.36% for bilateral lateral ventricles.
Yes—among older adults with advanced cancer in phase I trials, a higher symptom burden was associated with worse outcomes.

In a retrospective chart review of 56 phase I participants >60 years, those with >3 symptoms vs ≤3 had more admissions (37.5% vs 14.29%; P=.0335), more complications (46.43% vs 16.07%; P=.0026), and greater functional decline (24 vs 8 participants; P=.0173), while age >65 vs 60-65 showed no significant differences.
The supplied passages do not provide comparable symptom-burden data for younger phase I patients or establish symptoms as a formal selection criterion.

Yes, responsibility affects the public's valuation of health care interventions, but not uniformly: in a UK survey, participants valued preventing hospital-acquired infections, a health-care-caused harm, more highly than genetic disorders (1.31 vs 1.0).
The study elicited preferences from 1,030 people reflecting the UK sociodemographic mix, comparing interventions of equal cost and equal health benefit per person that differed by causation.

However, drug errors were valued similarly to genetic disorders (1.07), and preventing injuries to health care staff was valued less (0.71), as were lifestyle-related harms (0.65) and sports injuries (0.41), so the effect of responsibility depends on the type of intervention.
Yes, some pediatric type II supracondylar humerus fractures can be treated nonoperatively.

In a prospective registry of 259 pediatric type II SCHFs, 150 (57.9%) were ultimately treated nonoperatively and 109 (42.1%) surgically, with 39 initially nonoperative cases requiring surgery for unsatisfactory alignment.
At final follow-up, change in carrying angle, range of motion, and complications did not differ clinically significantly between treatment groups.

Fractures without rotational deformity or coronal angulation and with a shaft-condylar angle >15 degrees, or with isolated extension deformity alone, were more likely to be managed successfully without surgery.
The evidence is insufficient to regard pulp chamber pulpotomy as a permanent treatment.

In 17 patients aged 7-54 years with vital pulps and no clinical evidence of irreversible pulpitis, pulpotomy with ProRoot MTA had an estimated 82% survival without complementary treatment at 24 months.
Two of the 17 treated teeth required root canal treatment for pain control and one for prosthetic reasons.
Follow-up was only 12 to 24 months, so the data do not establish permanence.

The evidence is mixed/insufficient for the full comparison: in Florida's Medicaid Demonstration, provider service networks (PSNs) lowered per member per month (PMPM) expenditures by $7 more than HMOs among SSI enrollees, but the supplied passages do not compare PSNs with primary care case management. This finding rests on a difference-in-difference analysis of Florida Medicaid claims across two pre-Demonstration fiscal years and four post-Demonstration fiscal years, with 26,819,987 person-months. The same study also reported smaller savings among TANF enrollees and an overall lower PMPM increase in Demonstration counties ($40) than non-Demonstration counties ($186) among SSI enrollees, while no supplied passage reports expenditures for primary care case management.

Yes - pancreas retransplantation can give diabetic patients a second chance, based on a retrospective series of 37 second pancreas transplantations among 569 pancreas transplantations performed between 1976 and 2008, in which second-graft survival in the 17 patients transplanted from 1995 was close to primary graft survival of the whole population (71% vs.
79% at 1 year and 59% vs.
69% at 5 years; P=0.5075) and significantly better than those patients' own first pancreas survival (71% vs.
29% at 1 year and 59% vs.
7% at 5 years; P=0.0008), with similar results observed for all 37 retransplantations.
Patient survival was excellent (89% at 5 years), and pancreas retransplantation had no impact on kidney graft function or survival (100% at 5 years).

No, routine delayed-phase imaging in abdominopelvic CT is generally not worth the additional radiation based on a retrospective study of 1000 patients, in which delayed imaging was of no benefit in 958 (95.8%) and increased mean effective radiation dose by 59.5%.
The study included 1000 consecutive patients (912 men, 88 women; mean age 60 years) undergoing routine contrast-enhanced abdominopelvic CT, excluding examinations requiring multiphasic imaging.

Only 42 patients (4.2%) had findings further characterized or seen only on delayed phase, mostly incidental liver hemangiomas (n = 12), adrenal adenomas (n = 12), and parapelvic renal cysts (n = 6) that could have been confirmed at noninvasive follow-up, with the most important finding being a renal mass in one patient (0.1%).
The supplied passage does not report the additional time cost, so it does not settle that component of the question.
Pharmacologic regimens for knee osteoarthritis prevention can be cost-effective, but only in high-risk patients and under specific price and efficacy assumptions.

In a simulation model, base-case prophylaxis (initiated at age 50, 40% first-year efficacy, 0.22% major toxicity, $1,000/year) in the high-risk cohort (obese with prior knee injury) increased QALYs by 0.04 and lifetime costs by $4,600, yielding an ICER of $118,000 per QALY gained.
ICERs exceeded $150,000/QALY in the knee-injury-only cohort, and the regimen was less cost-effective than standard of care in obese-only and no-risk-factor cohorts.
Regimens priced at $3,000/year or more had ICERs above US cost-effectiveness thresholds.

The evidence is mixed/insufficient: in a cross-sectional validation study of 64 patients with clinician-diagnosed early-stage adhesive capsulitis, only 16 (25%) had a positive anesthetic response to intra-articular injection, and although global loss of passive range of movement (OR=0.26, P=.03), pain at end of range of all measured active movements (OR=0.06, P=.02), and global loss of passive glenohumeral movements (OR=0.23, P=.02) were initially associated with that response, only pain at end of range of all measured active movements remained after stepwise removal and was associated with reduced odds of a positive response.
The authors note that the lack of a recognized reference standard for diagnosing early-stage adhesive capsulitis remains problematic , and another source notes the diagnoses are clinician based.
Thus the passages do not show that the proposed clinical identifiers reliably capture the real picture of early-stage primary/idiopathic adhesive capsulitis.
Yes.

In a registry analysis of 5,400 laparoscopic sleeve gastrectomies, male gender, higher BMI, concomitant sleep apnea, conversion to laparotomy, longer operation time, use of both buttresses and oversewing, and intraoperative complications were associated with significantly higher staple line leak rates, while only operation time and year of procedure remained significant on multivariate analysis.
The same study reported the leak rate decreased from 6.5% to 1.4% during the study period.
Swine experiments suggest increased intragastric pressure, regional ischemia, and technical stapling failure as mechanisms, but they do not provide patient-level risk factors.
A separate study of gastrointestinal anastomotic dehiscence found standard risk stratifiers did not predict leakage, but it was not specific to primary sleeve gastrectomy.
No—based on the supplied study, resected stomach volume was not significantly related to weight loss after laparoscopic sleeve gastrectomy.

In 100 patients undergoing LSG divided into three groups by resected stomach volume (700–1,200 mL, n=21; 1,200–1,700 mL, n=62; >1,700 mL, n=17), mean percentage excess body weight loss at 3, 6, 12, and 24 months showed no significant differences among the groups.
Mean %EBWL at those times was 37.68%, 50.97%, 62.35%, and 67.59%, respectively.

Resected stomach volume was greater in patients with higher preoperative BMI and was positively associated with resected stomach weight, but the passages do not show a relationship between resected volume and weight loss.

Yes—emergency ultrasound (EUS) fellowship programs appear to impact emergency medicine (EM) residents' ultrasound education, based on a cross-sectional study of 244 EM residents at 9 academic medical centers.

Residents in programs with EUS fellowships reported performing more ultrasound scans than those in programs without fellowships (P =.04), and there were significant differences in most bedside ultrasound applications and in barriers to ultrasound education (P <.05).
However, the study is cross-sectional and does not establish causation or prove that fellowships enhance education; it shows associations with scan volume, scope, and barriers.
The evidence is insufficient to establish scintigraphy as a guideline method for determining amputation levels in diabetic foot.
One study of 30 diabetic foot patients used 3-phase bone scintigraphy to help mark the most distal perfused site as the amputation level, but it evaluated potential use rather than guideline status.
The other supplied passages address foot examinations or diabetic foot outcomes and do not mention scintigraphy for amputation-level determination.
Yes—in a randomized prospective study, more frequent skin care was associated with lower severity of incontinence-associated dermatitis.

Among 99 progressive care unit patients who were incontinent or had a fecal diversion/urinary catheter for more than 2 days, 55 received a defined skin care protocol every 6 hours and 44 received it every 12 hours, with both groups also receiving it as needed.
On discharge, the intervention group had a significantly lower moderate IAD dermatitis score (7.1%) than the control group (10.9%) (P ≤ 0.001).

Yes, early extubation should be a goal for most children after congenital cardiac surgery, based on a large series in which early extubation (≤24 hours) was achieved in 89% and was associated with lower mortality and reintubation.

In 613 children, including 97 neonates, undergoing congenital heart surgery, early extubation compared with delayed extubation was associated with lower mortality (1% vs 9%, P<.001) and lower reintubation (4% vs 23%, P<.001), while 71% were extubated intraoperatively and 89% within 24 hours.

However, this was a linked database analysis, not randomized, and predictors of delayed extubation included preoperative mechanical ventilation, weight <5 kg, longer procedure time, and postoperative inotrope support; Norwood operations had no patient extubated within 24 hours, so the goal should be individualized.
The other supplied passages are about preterm infants being weaned from ventilation and about physiologic monitoring around extubation after Fontan, so they do not settle the question.
The evidence is mixed: automated tailored prompts about family history risk led to some provider response but did not change downstream documentation or screening.

In 492 primary care patients aged 35-65 with moderate or strong familial risk for 6 diseases, 695 of 847 visits had a documented prompt response; 53.5% reviewed family history, 22.9% discussed it, 22.3% did not address it, and 0.7% reviewed and ordered tests/referrals.
However, there was no significant change in problem summary list documentation of risk status or screening interventions for any of the 6 diseases.
No, adding ganglionated plexi ablation to a Cox-Maze IV procedure was not beneficial for long-term stable sinus rhythm in the supplied evidence.

In 519 patients with persistent or long-standing persistent AF undergoing radiofrequency Maze IV, normal sinus rhythm off antiarrhythmic drugs at median 36.7 months was 75.5% without GP ablation versus 67.8% with GP ablation (p = 0.08).
Absence of GP ablation was not a significant predictor of AF recurrence (p = 0.12).
The evidence is mixed or insufficient to conclude that the altered maternal creatine homeostasis is a metabolic adaptation to pregnancy, though the study shows it is altered during gestation.

In pregnant spiny mice (n=8) compared with age-matched virgin females (n=6), plasma creatine and renal creatine excretion decreased significantly from mid to late gestation (P<0.001 and P<0.05, respectively), while term pregnancy increased lean tissue, kidney, liver, and heart mass (P<0.01, P<0.01, P<0.01, and P<0.05, respectively).

At term, creatine transporter expression increased in heart and skeletal muscle (P<0.05), heart and kidney creatine content increased (P<0.05 and P<0.001), and renal AGAT mRNA and protein were upregulated (P<0.01 and P<0.05), whereas CrT1 was downregulated in liver and brain (P<0.01) and AGAT/GAMT expression decreased in heart and brain.
The authors hypothesized these changes ensure adequate creatine for maternal tissues, placenta, and fetus, but the study was descriptive and did not directly test adaptiveness.
No, base deficit did not predict mortality in patients with isolated severe traumatic brain injury (TBI) in the supplied study.

In 108 patients over age 16 with isolated severe TBI, 88 (81.5%) had base deficit, but there was no statistically significant difference in mean base deficit between survivors and non-survivors, and the area under the ROC curve for base deficit as a predictor of mortality was statistically non-significant.
In a separate trauma population, a base deficit less than -15 was associated with 72% mortality versus 18.9% for 0 to -15, but this finding was not specific to severe TBI.
No, in elderly patients receiving small aortic valve prostheses, patient-prosthesis mismatch did not affect survival or quality of life.
In 152 patients aged at least 75 years with pure aortic stenosis who underwent aortic valve replacement with 19 or 21 mm valves, PPM occurred in 78 patients (53.8%).
Five-year overall survival was 78 ± 4.5% and was not influenced by PPM (P = NS), and quality-of-life scores were similar between PPM and no-PPM patients (P = NS).
Evidence from western China indicates that many tuberculosis patients are not fully adherent: 36.0% of newly confirmed TB patients experienced non-adherence during treatment.

In a prospective cohort of 481 new TB patients in three counties in western China followed from 2012 to 2013, non-adherence was defined as missing at least one drug dose or one follow-up re-examination, and 173 patients (36.0%) met this definition, with 136 (28.2%) lost to follow-up.
Only 13.9% took drugs under direct observation, while 60.5% were supervised by phone calls.
The other supplied passages do not address adherence among TB patients in China, as they concern extrapulmonary TB treatment duration and direct observation in an Indian drug-resistant TB program.
The evidence is mixed and insufficient to recommend for or against surgical treatment of lower limb fractures in patients with chronic spinal injuries.

In one study of 37 lower limb fractures in patients with chronic spinal cord injuries, 25 treated surgically and 12 orthopaedically, the surgical group had better clinical results, range of motion, bone consolidation, and less pressure ulcers and radiological misalignment, with no differences in pain, hospital stay, or medical complications.
However, the same report notes no consensus on management and a trend toward conservative treatment due to high complication rates with surgery.
The other supplied passages focus on trauma triage and CT imaging and do not address this question.

Yes, overexpression of Ki-67 is a prognostic biomarker of upper tract urinary carcinoma, based on a study showing high Ki-67 expression was associated with muscle-invasive tumors and poorer cancer-specific survival (CSS) and disease-free survival (DFS).

In that UTUC population, multivariate analysis found Ki-67 an independent prognostic factor for CSS (HR=3.196) and DFS (HR=3.517), and a meta-analysis of 12 studies with 1740 patients reported pooled HRs of 2.081 for poor survival and 2.791 for disease progression.
Subgroup pooled HRs were significant for CSS (2.276), metastasis-free survival (3.008), and DFS (6.336).
The evidence is insufficient to establish a direct implication for anal incontinence, though immunohistochemistry shows steroid hormone receptors in some anal canal tissues.

In 21 patients (14 women, 7 men), estrogen receptors were found in internal sphincter smooth muscle of all females (10/10) and 4/7 males, and in perimuscular connective tissue of all females (12/12) and 4/7 males, while no specific ER or PR staining occurred in external sphincter striated muscle (n=8).
In females, about 50% of ER-positive tissues were also PR-positive, and among males only one had PR staining confined to smooth muscle.

Because a hormonal influence on anal continence requires receptors in anal canal tissues, these findings suggest possible hormone responsiveness of the internal sphincter but not the external sphincter, yet the study did not measure anal incontinence outcomes.

The evidence is mixed: a prospective follow-up found no significant difference in rate of cognitive decline between subjects with and without hippocampal atrophy on MRI , while another study reported that right hippocampal size accounted for a significant portion of variance in cognitive scores.

In the prospective study, 5 controls, 7 depressed subjects, and 12 probable AD patients with HCA were compared with equal numbers without HCA and followed about 2 years with the Cambridge Cognitive Examination, and no significant differences in cognitive decline, mortality, or progression to dementia were found.
The third passage describes a method for measuring annual rate of hippocampal atrophy but reports no results linking it to cognitive decline.
Yes, the evidence suggests lunar position influences the time of delivery, based on a retrospective study of 1248 spontaneous full-term deliveries over 36 lunar months.

That analysis found a connection between the distribution of spontaneous full-term deliveries and the lunar month, with the effect of moon phases particularly relevant in multiparae and plurigravidae, where the mean day of delivery corresponded to the first or second day after the full moon.
However, the study was retrospective and does not establish causality.
No, the Child Health Computing System did not adequately identify children with cerebral palsy in the available comparison.

In children with cerebral palsy aged 5-9 years in one Health and Social Services Board in Northern Ireland, 47% of the 135 cases recorded on the Northern Ireland Cerebral Palsy Register were not found on the Child Health Computing System, and most of those missing children had no computer record of any medical diagnosis.
Among the 82 cases recorded on the Child Health Computing System, 12% were not on the register, and 6% were later found not to have CP, indicating both under-ascertainment and some misclassification.
